title: Serving incident orchestration for model degradations
author: Asha Kapoor
body:
Summary:
This playbook describes orchestration, runbooks, communications, and post-incident practices for operational incidents that manifest as model degradations: sustained latency regressions, throughput collapses, KV-cache corruption, and measurable model-quality regressions (e.g., hallucination rate or prompt-set failures). It focuses on incidents affecting Redwood inference serving (hosted, dedicated, private) and assumes responders have access to the Console, telemetry dashboards, and the serving runtime control plane.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: incidents where one or more model endpoints or model variants experience degraded performance or quality that impacts customer SLOs or causes meaningful customer errors.
- Intent: provide a repeatable, low-friction path from detection to recovery and learning. Priorities are: safety (prevent customer data loss), restore service (meet SLOs), reduce blast radius, and learn.

Classification matrix (severity mapping):
1) Sev1 — Full service outage or >50% of requests failing or >2x median latency across all regions for >5 minutes. Immediate bridge and customer notification.
2) Sev2 — Significant degradation for a subset of customers or a single region (e.g., sustained 5–10x p95 latency increase, backlog growth). Start bridge within 15 min.
3) Sev3 — Localized quality regressions (model outputs failing quality checks), slow error increases, non-customer-visible degradations. Begin triage during working hours.

Roles & responsibilities:
- Incident Commander (IC): owns orchestration, communications, and triage prioritization. Typically on-call service owner or SRE.
- Service Owner: primary model/endpoint engineer. Owns technical mitigation and rollback.
- Bridge Operator: runs the conference bridge / status page updates.
- Escalation Liaison (Customer Success): handles customer comms for enterprise customers.
- On-call Data Scientist: validates model-quality regressions and run evaluation harnesses.

Detection & initial signals (examples):
- Alerts: p95 latency > 2× baseline for 5 minutes; error-rate spike > 1% absolute; KV-cache miss rate > 20% leading to CPU/GPU increase.
- Console signals: per-route token-rate drop, sudden increase in request retries, or autoscaler thrash events.
- Quality monitors: prompt-set eval failure rate > 4% on production canary.
- Customer reports via support or status page.

Incident lifecycle (high-level steps):
1) Detect and declare incident: responder acknowledges alert in 5 minutes. If metrics cross Sev1 thresholds, IC declares Sev1.
2) Stand up bridge: Bridge Operator starts bridge (Zoom/Meet) and ticket in tracker (include live links).
3) Initial triage (first 15 minutes): determine blast radius, rollback options, safe mitigations.
4) Mitigate & restore (15–90 minutes): apply short-term mitigation (route traffic away, scale up reserved pool, swap model variant).
5) Stabilize & monitor (90–240 minutes): watch SLOs return to normal across 2× measurement window.
6) Close & learn (post-recovery): IC assigns postmortem owner within 24 hours.

Runbook: high-latency spike affecting hosted endpoints (quick checklist)
1) Evidence collection (first 5 min):
   - Check Console: per-model p50/p95/p99, active requests, queue length.
   - Run: Grafana query for p95 by region and model: "sum by(region, model) (histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[2m]) ))"
   - Check autoscaler events: rapid scale-outs/scale-ins.
2) Immediate mitigations (choose one based on blast radius):
   - Route traffic to a compatible model variant with known performance profile. Command: rdctl route set --route <route-id> --variant <variant-id> --weight 100
   - Pin customers to Dedicated pools if available: Console -> Customers -> Fast Switch -> Dedicated
   - Temporarily disable streaming/chunking on heavy routes to reduce scheduling overhead.
3) If KV-cache miss storm detected:
   - Rehydrate hot prefix caches: exec on cache-repopulate job: kubectl -n serving run cache-repop --image=infra/cache-pop --env PREFIX_LIST=/opt/hot-prefixes
   - If cache corruption suspected, pause writes and roll forward from last known-good snapshot: rdctl cache restore --snapshot <snapshot-id>
4) If autoscaler thrash:
   - Lock min/max pool sizes for the affected pool to current safe values via infra control plane.
   - Temporarily switch to reserved capacity for critical customers.
5) When latency is reduced to within SLO for 2 consecutive 5-minute windows, begin controlled rollback of temporary mitigations.

Runbook: model-quality regression (e.g., hallucination or prompt-set failures)
1) Triage classifier: check evaluation harness for failing prompt sets and production canary outputs.
2) If regression is only in a canary: stop rollout and revert to previous model variant.
3) If regression is in production: throttle traffic, enable safe-mode (strict decoding constraints, lower temperature), and route high-value customers to vetted variants.
4) Data collection: collect 1k sample inputs/outputs, flag for red-team review, and run against eval harness.

SLOs & thresholds (reference):
- Generation latency SLO (p95): 500ms for hosted small models, 1.2s for long-context variants.
- Availability: 99.9% monthly for hosted API (critical routes).
- Model-quality guardrail: canary pass rate >= 98% on core prompt-set.
- Alert thresholds: p95 > 2× baseline for 5m -> Sev2; p95 > 3× baseline for 5m or error-rate > 5% -> Sev1.

Communications templates (status page & enterprise notice):
- Status page short: "Degradation affecting text-generation endpoints in us-west-2. Engineers investigating. Some customers may experience elevated latency or failures. Updates at 30-minute cadence."
- Enterprise template (first notice):
  Subject: Incident affecting inference latency (US-West)
  Body: "We are currently investigating an incident impacting inference latency for model <model-name> in US-West. Impact: elevated p95 latency and increased request errors for a subset of requests. Actions: routing traffic to alternate variants and scaling dedicated pools for impacted customers. ETA for next update: 30 minutes. If you require a dedicated channel, reply to this message and we will open a customer bridge."
- Internal bridge message (standup):
  "IC: <name>. Current status: Sev2. Impact: p95 x5 for route /v1/generate. Mitigations in progress: variant swap and cache rehydration. Owner: <service-owner>. Next update in 15 minutes."

Postmortem template (required fields) — publish within 72h:
- Title (one-line)
- Incident ID
- Severity
- Timeline (UTC) with bullet timestamps
- Impact (customers, routes, metrics)
- Root cause analysis (technical and organizational factors)
- Mitigations applied during incident
- Remediation plan (owner + ETA)
- Follow-ups and action items (owner, due date, verification steps)
- Postmortem reviewers

On-call rotations, handoffs, and expectations:
- Primary on-call: 1-week rotation (Mon 09:00 UTC -> next Mon 09:00 UTC). SREs and owners swap weekly.
- Secondary/reserve: assigned for 24/7 coverage escalation.
- Handoff checklist (before shift end): active incidents, outstanding actions, customer escalations, link to bridge and runbook, list of temporary mitigations.
- Quiet window: prefer handoffs outside of expected maintenance or game-day windows.

Game day plan (quarterly, 90–120 minutes exercise)
- Objective: validate detection and response to a model-quality regression introduced in a canary rollout and a simultaneous KV-cache miss storm.
- Participants: on-call SRE, service owner, on-call data scientist, customer liaison, bridge operator.
- Scenario steps:
  1) Seed canary with failing prompt-set (automated).
  2) Trigger cache eviction on a test pool.
  3) Observe alerts (must fire within 5 minutes) and require team to follow runbook.
  4) Evaluate time-to-recovery and communications.
- Scoring: detection (0–5), triage accuracy (0–5), mitigation correctness (0–10), communications clarity (0–5).

Operational tooling & quick commands (reference):
- rdctl list models --region us-west-2
- rdctl swap-variant --route <route> --from <old> --to <new>
- kubectl -n serving logs -l app=runtime --since=10m | grep "backpressure"
- grafana link: Console -> Dashboards -> Serving -> p95 by model

Runbook hygiene and ownership:
- Every runbook section must have an owner and a last-reviewed date. This playbook is reviewed quarterly by the Eng SRE and Serving Runtime teams.
- Postmortem owners must close follow-ups or convert them into roadmap tickets within 30 days.

Appendix A — example evidence table (for postmortem)
| Item | Where to find | Example query/command | Notes |
| Timeline logs | /var/log/serving/events | grep "2027-02-09T" /var/log/serving/events | include request ids |
| Metrics | Grafana serving cluster | see dashboard: p95-by-model | export CSV at time window |
| Cache snapshot | S3://redwood-cache/snapshots/ | rdctl cache list-snapshots | pick most recent <snapshot-id> |

Appendix B — escalation matrix quick reference:
- 0–15 minutes: on-call primary (ack & bridge)
- 15–45 minutes: SRE + service owner engage; escalate to IC if unresolved
- >45 minutes or customer-impacting SEV1: Paging to Engineering Director and Customer Success lead.

References & related pages:
- Serving runtime architecture (link): /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture
- SLO and error budget playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets
- Model onboarding and QA: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding

Document history:
- 2026-11-15: Created by Asha Kapoor
- 2027-02-10: Reviewed and published after game-day validation (reviewers: Miguel Santos, Riley Chen, Priya Nair)

This document is intended as an operational reference. If you are the on-call first responder, follow the shortest path to restore service and then enable learning via the postmortem template.
